questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes what Layer 2 (Data Link) of the OSI model is responsible for, as Lesson 1 defines it?
options: Organizing bits into frames and adding physical (MAC) addressing — switches operate at this layer
Logical addressing and routing between networks, where routers operate
End-to-end delivery between two specific applications using port numbers
Moving raw bits as electrical signals, light pulses, or radio waves, with no understanding of addresses
Translating data into a format both ends agree on, including encryption such as TLS
Opening, maintaining, and tearing down the conversation between two applications
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines Layer 2 (Data Link) as the layer that organizes bits into frames and adds physical addressing — the MAC address burned into a network card — which is exactly where switches operate, forwarding frames based on MAC address rather than IP address.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes Layer 1 (Physical), not Layer 2 — moving raw bits as electrical signals, light, or radio waves with no understanding of addressing is explicitly Lesson 1's description of the Physical layer. Layer 2 adds the frame structure and MAC addressing on top of those bits; confusing the two is exactly the mix-up the lesson's layer-by-layer breakdown is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 2, as data moves down the stack toward the wire, each layer ________ the data from the layer above it in its own header, and the reverse process at the receiving end is called de-encapsulation.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 describes encapsulation as each layer wrapping the layer above it's data in its own header — application data gets wrapped in a TCP segment, then an IP packet, then an Ethernet frame — and de-encapsulation is each layer stripping its own header back off at the receiving end.

questions.prompt: Match each network topology from Lesson 3 to what it actually is.
right: Connects each device to exactly two neighbors, forming a closed loop that traffic travels around
Connects every device to multiple other devices directly, providing redundancy at the cost of cabling scale
Connects every device individually to a central switch, so one cable failing only takes down that one device
Connects every device to a single shared cable, where one break can take down the entire network
questions.explain: Star topology connects every device to a central switch, so a single cable failure is isolated to one device. Bus topology shares one cable among all devices, so one break can disable the whole network. Ring topology connects each device to exactly two neighbors in a closed loop. Mesh topology connects devices directly to multiple others, which is why a full mesh of even 10 devices needs 45 connections, per Lesson 3.

questions.prompt: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC address is not yet in its MAC address table. Per Lesson 4, what does the switch do with that frame?
options: Floods it out every port except the one it arrived on, until it learns which port the destination lives on
Drops the frame immediately since the destination can't be confirmed
Sends the frame back to the source marked as unreachable
Forwards the frame only to the device's default gateway
questions.explain: Lesson 4 describes flooding as the switch's behavior when it doesn't yet know which port a destination MAC lives on: it sends the frame out every port except the one it arrived on, a one-time broadcast-like behavior that stops once the switch learns the real port from that device's own reply.

questions.prompt: For the subnet 192.168.1.0/26 worked through in Lesson 5, what is the correct network address, broadcast address, and usable host range?
options: Network 192.168.1.0, broadcast 192.168.1.63, usable range 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.62
Network 192.168.1.0, broadcast 192.168.1.255, usable range 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.254
Network 192.168.1.1, broadcast 192.168.1.62, usable range 192.168.1.2 through 192.168.1.61
questions.explain: Lesson 5 works this exact subnet: a /26 leaves 6 host bits (2^6 = 64 total addresses). The network address is all host bits 0 (192.168.1.0), the broadcast address is all host bits 1 (192.168.1.63), and the usable host range is everything in between — 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.62 — since the network and broadcast addresses are never assignable to a host.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 6, a run of consecutive all-zero groups in an IPv6 address can be replaced with ________, but only once per address, since using it twice would make the address ambiguous.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 explains that the :: shorthand replaces one run of consecutive all-zero groups in an IPv6 address. It can only appear once per address — using it twice would leave no way to tell how many zero groups belong in each gap, making the address ambiguous.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about routing, per Lesson 7.
options: A router picks the most specific matching route in its routing table, so a /32 route beats a /24 route, which beats the default /0 route
A default gateway is the router a device sends traffic to when the destination isn't on its own local subnet
Static routes automatically recalculate paths whenever a link goes down
OSPF and EIGRP are examples of Exterior Gateway Protocols
BGP is the protocol that effectively holds the entire internet's routing together between separate autonomous systems
questions.explain: Lesson 7 explains that routers always pick the most specific matching entry, and a default gateway is exactly what a device relies on for any destination outside its own subnet. BGP is the exterior gateway protocol tying the internet's autonomous systems together. Static routes are the opposite of adaptive — they require a human to notice and fix a failed link — and OSPF/EIGRP are named in the lesson as Interior, not Exterior, Gateway Protocols.

questions.prompt: Put DHCP's DORA process, from Lesson 8, in the correct order.
items: Client broadcasts Discover, asking if any DHCP server is out there
Server responds with Offer, proposing an IP address the client can use
Client broadcasts Request, saying it will take that IP address
Server sends Acknowledge, confirming the IP is leased to the client
questions.explain: Lesson 8 walks through DORA as a four-step exchange: Discover (the client asking), Offer (a server proposing an address), Request (the client claiming that address), and Acknowledge (the server confirming the lease) — each step depends on the one before it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines UDP, as distinguished from TCP in Lesson 9?
options: Connectionless, "fire-and-forget" delivery with no handshake, no sequence numbers, and no guarantee of delivery or order
Connection-oriented delivery that performs a three-way handshake before any application data is sent
A protocol that retransmits any segment that isn't acknowledged in time
A protocol that buffers out-of-order segments and reassembles the original order before handing data to the application
A protocol used exclusively for file transfer, never for DNS queries or streaming video
A protocol that guarantees every byte sent will arrive in the order it was sent, or the connection reports failure
questions.explain: Lesson 9 defines UDP as connectionless and "fire-and-forget": no handshake, no sequence numbers, no retransmission. A host just sends a datagram and moves on, trading guaranteed delivery for lower overhead and lower latency — which is exactly why DNS queries, streaming video, and VoIP calls choose it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes TCP, not UDP — the three-way handshake, sequence-number tracking, and guaranteed in-order delivery described in options B, C, D, and F are precisely the overhead TCP pays for reliability that Lesson 9 says UDP deliberately skips. Swapping which protocol does the handshaking is exactly the mix-up this lesson is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 10, an internal workstation making an outbound connection to an unfamiliar external IP on port ________ is a red flag worth investigating, because that port number points to SMB — a protocol frequently targeted for lateral movement.
questions.explain: Lesson 10's memorized port table lists 445 as SMB, Windows' file and printer sharing protocol, and specifically calls it out as a common lateral-movement target — exactly the kind of connection a SOC analyst flags for review.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about web, email, and file-transfer services, per Lesson 11.
options: HTTPS wraps the same request/response exchange as HTTP inside a TLS-encrypted tunnel
SMTP is the protocol used to retrieve email you've already received
IMAP keeps the mailbox synced across every device you check it from, while POP3 downloads messages and typically removes them from the server
SFTP tunnels file transfer through SSH's encryption, protecting credentials and file contents in transit
FTP encrypts login credentials by default, making it a secure choice on an untrusted network
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is explicit that HTTPS is the same HTTP conversation wrapped in TLS, that IMAP syncs across devices while POP3 downloads and removes mail, and that SFTP is the SSH-encrypted secure replacement for FTP. SMTP is specifically the protocol that sends and relays mail, not retrieves it, and FTP sends everything — including credentials — in plaintext, which is exactly why it's considered insecure.

questions.prompt: An attacker captures a WPA2 network's 4-way handshake and runs an offline dictionary attack against the captured data. Per Lesson 12, why doesn't that same approach work against a WPA3 network using SAE?
options: WPA3 replaces the password exchange with SAE (the "dragonfly" handshake), which is specifically resistant to offline dictionary attacks against a captured exchange
WPA3 networks never perform any kind of handshake at all
WPA3 uses the exact same 4-way handshake as WPA2, just paired with a longer minimum password length
WPA3 prevents an attacker from capturing any wireless traffic whatsoever
questions.explain: Lesson 12 explains that WPA3's SAE handshake directly addresses WPA2's biggest weakness — a captured 4-way handshake that's vulnerable to offline dictionary or brute-force attacks against the password. SAE is built to resist exactly that offline attack, and WPA3 also adds forward secrecy so even a later-compromised password can't retroactively decrypt earlier traffic.

questions.prompt: Match each security control from Lesson 13 to which leg(s) of the CIA triad it protects.
right: Protects availability by letting another server take over if one dies or gets flooded
Protects integrity by letting you detect if even a single bit of a file or message was altered
Protects confidentiality, because even if the data is intercepted, it can't be read
Protects both confidentiality and integrity by stopping an unauthorized party from reading or changing data
questions.explain: Lesson 13 maps each control back to the triad: encryption protects confidentiality, hashing and digital signatures protect integrity, redundancy/backups/DDoS mitigation protect availability, and strong access controls like MFA protect more than one leg at once — stopping unauthorized reading and unauthorized changing in the same step.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about threat actors, per Lesson 14.
options: A nation-state actor is typically associated with highly sophisticated, well-resourced "advanced persistent threats"
An insider threat has to break into the network first, the same way an external attacker does
A script kiddie typically runs attack tools someone else built without fully understanding them
Organized crime groups are primarily motivated by ideology rather than financial profit
The attack surface includes things that aren't obviously "IT," like a vendor's weak password or a forgotten test server
questions.explain: Lesson 14 explicitly ties nation-state actors to APTs and describes script kiddies as running tools they don't fully understand. It also stresses that the attack surface is bigger than people assume, including non-obvious things like a vendor's weak password. An insider threat is uniquely dangerous precisely because they already have legitimate access and never need to break in, and organized crime is described as financially motivated, not ideological.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 15, risk is often expressed informally as Risk = Likelihood × ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 defines risk as combining a threat and a vulnerability with consequence: the likelihood that a given threat exploits a given vulnerability, multiplied by the impact if it does — Risk = Likelihood × Impact.

questions.prompt: Put the seven stages of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, from Lesson 16, in the correct order.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 lays out the kill chain as a progression: the attacker researches the target (Reconnaissance), builds the tool (Weaponization), gets it to the target (Delivery), triggers it (Exploitation), installs persistence (Installation), opens a remote channel (Command & Control), and finally does what they came to do (Actions on Objectives).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why a password plus a security-question answer does NOT count as true multi-factor authentication, per Lesson 17?
options: Both are "something you know," the same factor category, so proving one doesn't meaningfully prove possession of a genuinely different kind of factor
Security questions are biometric, so pairing one with a password mixes "something you know" with "something you are"
MFA always requires exactly three factors, and a password plus a security question is only two
A security-question answer counts as "something you have," so this combination already qualifies as true MFA
Security questions are never actually used in real authentication systems
MFA only applies to hardware security keys and never covers knowledge-based methods at all
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit that two factors from the same category don't count as real MFA — a password plus a security-question answer is "something you know," twice, and someone who can guess or find one can often find the other, adding little real protection. True MFA requires factors from different categories.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D wrongly classifies a security-question answer as "something you have." Per Lesson 17, a security question is a memorized secret — exactly like a password — so it belongs to "something you know," the same category as the password itself, not a different one. Mislabeling which factor category something belongs to is exactly the error this lesson's three-factor breakdown is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 18 to what it actually is.
right: Deciding what an already-authenticated user is allowed to do
Permissions tied to a job role, assigned via group or profile membership
The resource's owner decides who gets access, and can change that decision at any time
Centrally enforced labels and clearance levels that even the resource's owner cannot override
questions.explain: Lesson 18 distinguishes authorization (what an authenticated user may do) from the three access-control models: RBAC ties permissions to a role, DAC lets the resource's owner decide, and MAC enforces centrally-assigned labels that even the owner can't override.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19, why does TLS bother using slow asymmetric encryption at all, instead of using fast symmetric encryption for the entire connection?
options: Asymmetric encryption solves the key-exchange problem by securely exchanging a session key during the handshake, after which TLS switches to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the connection
Asymmetric encryption is actually faster than symmetric encryption for large volumes of data
Symmetric encryption cannot be used at all once a TLS connection has been opened
TLS uses asymmetric encryption for the entire connection and never switches to symmetric encryption
questions.explain: Lesson 19 explains that TLS uses asymmetric encryption briefly, during the handshake, to safely exchange a freshly generated symmetric session key — solving the key-exchange problem once, up front — and then switches to fast symmetric encryption, using that session key, for the rest of the connection.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 20, ________ is the real-world standard hash algorithm most commonly used today, always producing a 256-bit output no matter how large or small the input is.
questions.explain: Lesson 20 names SHA-256 as the real-world standard hashing algorithm, always producing a fixed 256-bit digest regardless of input size — the basis for both safe password storage and file-integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about malware types, per Lesson 21.
options: A virus requires a human to execute the host file it's attached to before it can spread
A worm needs a host file to attach to, the same way a virus does
A trojan self-replicates across a network the same way a worm does
Ransomware is defined by its goal — encrypting data and demanding payment — rather than by one specific delivery method
The 2017 WannaCry outbreak spread machine-to-machine without needing anyone to click anything, which is a defining worm behavior
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that a virus can't travel without a human executing its host file, that ransomware is defined by its goal rather than its delivery method, and that WannaCry's machine-to-machine spread with no user action is exactly the worm behavior the lesson describes. A worm specifically does NOT need a host file, and a trojan's defining trait is deception, not self-replication — it relies on the user willingly installing it.

questions.prompt: An attacker calls the IT help desk claiming to be a VP traveling overseas who urgently needs a password reset over the phone, with no video call or ID check. Per Lesson 22, which technique is this, and what makes it work?
options: Pretexting — the fabricated scenario (a traveling executive) combined with urgency gives the target a plausible reason to break a rule they'd normally follow
Baiting — the attacker is offering something enticing to trigger a compromise
Spear phishing — the attacker researched the target's writing style before sending the email
Mass phishing — the attacker is targeting thousands of recipients at once with this call
questions.explain: Lesson 22 describes pretexting as exactly this scenario: a fabricated identity or situation, often paired with urgency or a claim of authority, that gives the target a plausible reason to break a rule they'd normally follow — like resetting a password with no identity verification.

questions.prompt: A target receives an overwhelming flood of traffic, but every packet traces back to the exact same source IP address. Per Lesson 23, is this most consistent with a DoS or a DDoS attack, and why?
options: A DoS attack — the defining trait of DoS is that the flood comes from a single source, unlike DDoS, which comes from many sources at once
A DDoS attack — any traffic flood large enough to overwhelm a target is automatically classified as distributed
A DoS attack — DoS can only be identified by the size of the payload, never by the number of source IPs involved
A DDoS attack — a single source IP flooding a target is actually the textbook definition of "distributed"
questions.explain: Lesson 23 draws the DoS/DDoS line specifically on source count: DoS floods from a single source, while DDoS floods from many sources at once, typically a botnet. One consistent source IP points directly to DoS, not DDoS.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 24, both SQL injection and Cross-Site Scripting trace back to the same root cause — a web application trusting user ________ instead of validating or sanitizing it first.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 identifies the shared root cause behind SQL injection and XSS as a web application using data a user typed directly, without checking or cleaning it first — trusting input instead of validating it.

questions.prompt: A company has a firewall, antivirus, and strong passwords, but every one of those controls is managed by the same single IT contractor using the same default settings across the board. Per Lesson 25, is this real defense in depth?
options: No — true defense in depth requires layers that fail for different reasons; controls sharing the same management and default settings share the same blind spots, making them one layer repeated rather than several independent ones
Yes — having three different types of controls (firewall, antivirus, passwords) automatically counts as defense in depth regardless of how they're managed
Yes — defense in depth is only about the number of tools deployed, not how independently they're managed
No — defense in depth requires at least five layers, and this company only has three
Yes — as long as a password policy exists, any additional control counts as a second independent layer
No — defense in depth doesn't apply to small companies, only to large enterprises
questions.explain: Lesson 25 is explicit that defense in depth is about independence of failure, not just the number of tools: layers should fail for different reasons, built and managed somewhat independently. One contractor applying the same default settings to every control means they likely share the same blind spot, making them effectively one layer with backup copies rather than several genuinely independent ones.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B assumes that having three different categories of tool automatically means independent layers. Lesson 25 directly rejects this logic with its own analogy: buying ten firewalls doesn't give you defense in depth, it's one layer repeated. The lesson's actual test is whether the layers fail for different reasons, not whether they're different products — and the same contractor applying the same default settings to all three fails that test.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about security policy, per Lesson 26.
options: An Acceptable Use Policy defines what employees are and aren't allowed to do with company systems and data
A password policy becomes an actual enforced technical control once IT configures the identity provider's settings to match what the policy specifies
An incident response policy is written during the incident itself, not ahead of time
A data classification policy defines categories like public, internal, confidential, and restricted, along with handling rules for each
Written security policy is unnecessary once technical controls are already configured
questions.explain: Lesson 26 describes the AUP and data classification policy exactly this way, and walks through the password-policy example to show how a written requirement becomes an enforced technical setting once IT configures it. An incident response policy is specifically meant to be written ahead of time — without it, the first hours of a real incident get spent arguing about process — and policy is described as the single source of truth technical controls are configured against, not something that becomes unnecessary once controls exist.

questions.prompt: Match each NIST Cybersecurity Framework function from Lesson 27 to what it actually covers.
right: Contain and act on a detected incident
Know your assets, systems, data, and the risks to them
Find security events as they happen
Put safeguards in place, such as access control and training
questions.explain: Lesson 27 lays out the NIST Cybersecurity Framework's functions: Identify means knowing your assets and risks, Protect means the safeguards from the layered defense model, Detect means finding events as they happen, and Respond means containing and acting on a detected incident — directly mapping onto the incident response policy from Lesson 26.

questions.prompt: Why does setting a lab VM's network adapter to "Bridged" defeat the purpose of building an isolated home lab, per Lesson 29?
options: Bridged mode exposes the VM directly on the real home network and the internet, instead of the Host-Only or Internal Network setting that keeps lab traffic contained to VMs on the same host
Bridged mode disables the VM's network adapter entirely, so no lab traffic can flow at all
Bridged mode is only available in VMware, never in VirtualBox, so it isn't a realistic option either way
Bridged mode automatically encrypts all lab traffic, which makes exploit practice unrealistic
questions.explain: Lesson 29 is explicit that Bridged exposes a VM directly on the real home network and the internet, which is exactly what a lab with live exploit traffic must avoid. Host-Only (VirtualBox) or Internal Network (VMware) is what creates a private virtual network that only the lab VMs can see, keeping practice traffic from ever reaching the real router or the wider internet.

questions.prompt: In a Wireshark capture, one source IP sends SYN packets to twenty different destination ports on the same target within one second, and almost none of them get a SYN-ACK back. Per Lesson 30, what does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: A port scan — the scanning tool is checking which ports respond, which is why most attempts never complete with a SYN-ACK
A completed, healthy TCP three-way handshake repeating normally
A DNS query being resolved through its normal caching process
A single large file transfer being split across many simultaneous connections
questions.explain: Lesson 30 describes a port scan as exactly this pattern: one source IP sending SYN packets to many different destination ports in rapid succession, with most getting no SYN-ACK reply at all, because the scanning tool is simply checking which ports respond.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of Lesson 31's Fairmont Logistics case study in the order the attack actually unfolded.
items: Attacker runs an internet-wide scan and finds Fairmont's exposed ports (Reconnaissance)
Attacker sends a phishing email with a malicious Word document disguised as a vendor invoice (Weaponization & Delivery)
Employee opens the attachment and enables macros, executing malicious code (Exploitation)
Malicious code installs a backdoor that persists after reboot (Installation)
Backdoor beacons out to an attacker-controlled server at a steady interval (Command & Control)
Attacker exfiltrates customer records through the C2 channel (Actions on Objectives)
questions.explain: Lesson 31 traces Fairmont Logistics through the full kill chain: a reconnaissance scan finds exposed ports, a phishing email with a malicious attachment delivers the weapon, an enabled macro achieves exploitation, a persistent backdoor is installed, that backdoor beacons out to establish command and control, and only then does the attacker exfiltrate customer records — each stage building on the one before it, which is exactly why breaking any single link earlier is cheaper than cleaning up after the last one.
